roots.context: We counted sides and corners on paper shapes. Now let us think about where a shape's name comes from.

deep_truth.truth: In the Triangle Test, the thin piece and the upside-down piece did not look like triangles. But each had 3 straight sides and 3 corners. People agreed that this is what the word triangle means. So a shape gets its name from a rule that anyone can check by counting. Its size, its colour and the way it points are left out of the rule.
deep_truth.habit: We think we know a shape just by looking, the way we know a face. But the look can fool us. The name comes from a rule that people chose.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Triangle Test, five pieces that looked very different all had 3 beans and 3 straight sides. The piece with a curved side had 3 beans too, and still failed.

three.who_am_i: You can see a triangle in a samosa, a flag and a hanger. Your mind picks out what is the same in all three.
three.what_is_life: Other living beings make shapes too. A small pufferfish makes a big circle in the sand. Bees build wax cells with six sides.
three.what_is_this_world: No dosa is a perfect circle. Each one has small bumps. Real things only come close to the shapes we name.

roots.thread: A dosa, a bangle, a coin and the full Moon are four different things. We call all of them by one name: circle. So one shape shows up in many things. None of them is a perfect circle, and yet each one makes us think of it.

teachings.teaching: The Chandogya Upanishad says: if you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. A pot and a plate have different names, but both are clay.
teachings.link: Shape names work the other way round. A clay plate, a steel plate and a dosa are made of different things, and we give them one name, circle. A name picks out the part we choose to look at.

teachings.teaching: This old Greek letter is said to be by Plato, though scholars are not sure he wrote it. It says that every circle drawn by hand or made on a turning tool is a little bit wrong somewhere. The true circle is none of these.
teachings.link: The circle you drew round a bangle is very close, but it is not perfect. The letter says the perfect circle is real all the same. Others say it is an idea that minds make.

science.text: In 2006, scientists showed sets of six pictures to Mundurukú children and adults in the Amazon forest of Brazil. They had little or no schooling, and their language has few words for shapes. They still picked the odd shape out about two times in three (Dehaene and others, 2006). Scientists do not agree on what this shows about where our sense of shape comes from.
Is a perfect circle a real thing, or an idea that minds make? Nobody has settled this.

other_view.who: Many mathematicians, from the Greek thinker Plato onwards
other_view.view: They say people did not choose what a triangle is. Triangles were there to be found, like a mountain. People only chose the word. Three straight sides meet at three corners whether anyone agrees or not.

practice.title: Once round the rim
practice.say: Hold a steel tumbler or a bangle. Close your eyes. Put one finger on the rim. Breathe in slowly and move your finger half way round. Breathe out and come back to where you began. Do this five times. Then tell me. Where does the circle begin? Where does it end?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Move one finger slowly round the rim of a tumbler. Breathe in for half the way, and out for the rest. Where does the circle begin?

ask: Who decided that a triangle has three sides? Could they have chosen something else?
No dosa is a perfect circle. So where is the perfect circle?
A thin triangle and a wide triangle look different. Why do we give them the same name?
A pufferfish has no word for circle. Does he still know what he is making?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that children see shapes differently from grown-ups? This card tells the true story of two teachers and a later test.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, schoolbooks showed one kind of triangle. It sat flat, with its point on top. Teachers thought that a child who could name it knew what a triangle was. In 1957 two Dutch teachers, Dina van Hiele-Geldof and her husband Pierre van Hiele, wrote about what they had seen in their own classes. They said that learners first know a shape by its whole look, the way we know a face. Only later do they notice its sides and corners. Dina died the next year, in 1958, and for many years few people outside the Netherlands knew of the work. In 1999 four researchers in the United States, Douglas Clements, Sudha Swaminathan, Mary Anne Hannibal and Julie Sarama, tested the idea. They sat with 97 children aged 3 to 6, one at a time, and asked them to pick out shapes. Most of the children chose mainly by matching the look. So children need to meet many kinds of triangle, and to count the sides and corners for themselves.
how_we_found_out.who: Dina van Hiele-Geldof and Pierre van Hiele, and later Douglas Clements, Sudha Swaminathan, Mary Anne Hannibal and Julie Sarama
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A child who can name the usual triangle knows what a triangle is. The van Hieles in 1957, and the test with 97 children in 1999, showed that young children go mostly by the look. So they often leave out a thin or upside-down triangle.

van Hiele-Geldof, D. and van Hiele, P. M. (1957). Two doctoral theses at Utrecht University on levels of thinking in geometry. Dina van Hiele-Geldof lived from 1911 to 1958.

Kawase, H., Okata, Y. and Ito, K. (2013). Role of huge geometric circular structures in the reproduction of a marine pufferfish. Scientific Reports 3, 2106. (A circle about 2 metres wide, built in 7 to 9 days, off Amami-Oshima, Japan. The fish was later named Torquigener albomaculosus.)

Dehaene, S., Izard, V., Pica, P. and Spelke, E. (2006). Core knowledge of geometry in an Amazonian indigene group. Science 311, 381-384. (14 children and 30 adults, 43 sets of six pictures, about 67 in 100 right.)

Karihaloo, B. L., Zhang, K. and Wang, J. (2013). Honeybee combs: how the circular cells transform into rounded hexagons. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 10. The opposing view is by Bauer and Bienefeld (2013). A 2016 review in Scientific Reports called the question still open.
Euclid, Elements, Book I, Definition 22: the square and the oblong are listed as separate four-sided figures.

The Sulba Sutras: rope rules for laying out squares, rectangles and circles for fire altars. The oldest, linked to Baudhayana, is dated to about 800 to 500 BCE (MacTutor History of Mathematics archive).

Indian Roads Congress, IRC 67, Code of Practice for Road Signs: mandatory signs are mostly circular, cautionary signs triangular, informatory signs rectangular. Stop is an octagon and Give Way is a triangle pointing down.
Hopscotch in India: Paandi (Tamil Nadu), Kunte Bille (Karnataka), Tokkudu Billa (Andhra Pradesh and Telangana), from encyclopedia entries on the traditional games.
Tamil mukkonam (three, and konam for corner or angle). Hindi trikon (three corners) and tribhuj (three arms). Dictionary meanings were checked, but no etymological dictionary was consulted.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Triangle Test needs about 5 minutes of cutting by a grown-up. The tiny triangle must be at least matchbox size, or three beans will not fit on it. Beans and a finger give 3 and 3 for all five triangles, 3 corners with 2 straight sides for the cake slice, and 4 and 4 for the piece with its top cut off. In the Turn Test a hand-cut oval fits its outline once or twice, depending on how evenly it is cut, and the table says so. Fill the Shape Mat was played in the head with 1 and 2 players: about 12 rolls each, and nobody can get stuck because 5 and 6 are free choices. The sticks challenge was checked by counting: only 4, 8 and 12 sticks make a square, and sides of 3, 2 and 1 sticks fall flat. Paandi needs a floor you can chalk or tape, so it is outside the core path. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 1999 study of 97 children, the van Hiele theses of 1957, the pufferfish paper of 2013, the Mundurukú study of 2006, the honeycomb debate, Euclid's definition of the oblong, Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4, the circle passage in the Seventh Letter, the shapes of Indian road signs, the regional names of hopscotch and the age of the Sulba Sutras. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it. The shapes in the puzzles are drawn with text symbols such as ▲ and ■. Look at them once on your own phone to see that they show clearly.
